bipartite.note: The translation dissolves the sharp pivot from lived sensation (kami) to rhetorical accusation (shimo) into a single continuous first-person narrative of grief and slow dawn; the rhetorical question directed at the husband's ignorance is entirely absent, replaced by a subjective description of how slowly the hours seemed to pass. The bipartite boundary between the sensory kami and the accusatory shimo is lost — there's no 'does he know' address at all, just a report of feeling.

kakekotoba_handling.note: The translator renders 'night' purely as a temporal setting for the weeping/watching; the secondary sense of 'life/lot' as a marriage condition is not evoked anywhere in the six lines — there is no suggestion that this night stands for an enduring married state.

kigo_handling.note: Consistent with the source analysis, no seasonal word or seasonal atmosphere is present; the poem/translation concerns temporal grief (night into dawn) rather than any seasonal imagery, and Dickens introduces no seasonal substitution.

line_mapping.structural_note: Dickens expands the five ku into six flowing lines of continuous first-person lament, but crucially omits the shimo-no-ku's rhetorical address to the absent man (‘いかに久しきものとかは知る’ — does he know how long?), converting an implicit reproach into a purely descriptive statement of the speaker's own suffering; this removes the bipartite pivot from sensation to accusation.

Dickens.translator_strategy: Dickens prioritizes a smooth, emotionally expressive English lyric of solitary grief over preserving the original's rhetorical accusation, sacrificing the shimo-no-ku's pointed address to the negligent husband in favor of a continuous, decorative narrative of the woman's own weeping and the slow passage of night.

bipartite.note: The translation reverses the order of the source: it opens with the shimo-no-ku's rhetorical exclamation about the length of the wait ('What a long time / To the dawn') before presenting the kami-no-ku's sensory content of weeping and sleeping alone. The rhetorical-question form is also flattened into an exclamation, losing the pointed accusatory pivot toward the husband's ignorance, so the inferential-sensory logic (lived night experience -> demand for acknowledgment) is reduced to a simple emotional statement without the original's directed reproach.

kakekotoba_handling.note: The translation keeps 'night' only as the literal temporal setting ('When I weep through the night'); the secondary sense of 夜 as one's life/lot/married condition is not carried over — there is no suggestion that this single night stands for her enduring marital situation.

kigo_handling.note: As the source itself contains no seasonal marker, there is nothing seasonal to preserve or lose; the translation likewise contains no seasonal imagery, consistent with the source's kigo being 'none'.

The dawn/coming of day (明くる間)

Sleeping alone (ひとりぬる)

line_mapping.structural_note: The translator inverts the order of the original, front-loading the shimo-no-ku's emotional conclusion ('What a long time / To the dawn') before the kami-no-ku's sensory grounding ('weep through the night, / And sleep alone'), collapsing the rhetorical question about the husband's ignorance into a simple exclamatory statement and thus losing the accusatory pivot altogether.

Noguchi.translator_strategy: Noguchi prioritizes a compact, emotionally direct four-line lyric over structural fidelity, reordering the poem's clauses and converting its rhetorical accusation into a simple exclamation of grief.

bipartite.note: Porter dissolves the rhetorical-question pivot of the shimo-ku into a simple continuation of the speaker's lament rather than a pointed inferential accusation directed at the husband's ignorance. Lines 4-5 ('How weary I have grown / Of being left alone!') restate the speaker's own weariness rather than posing the bitter rhetorical question of whether the man understands the length of the wait; the accusatory/inferential logic aimed outward at the husband is lost, replaced by an inward-focused continuous complaint.

kakekotoba_handling.note: Porter renders 夜 straightforwardly as 'night' with added adjectives 'long and dreary,' capturing the literal temporal sense of the solitary night but giving no hint of the secondary sense of 夜 as standing for the speaker's whole marital 'life' or 'lot.' The pivot's double meaning collapses into a single literal image.

kigo_handling.note: The source analysis identifies no true seasonal marker in this poem (season: none), and Porter's translation likewise introduces no seasonal imagery; 'night' and 'dreary' function as emotional/temporal descriptors, not seasonal ones, consistent with the source's lack of kigo.

line_mapping.structural_note: Porter expands the five-line waka into a five-line English stanza but redistributes content: the kami-ku's sighing and solitary night are spread across lines 1-2, an entirely invented image of a 'desolate chamber' is added in line 3, and the shimo-ku's rhetorical question is replaced by lines 4-5 expressing the speaker's own weariness and loneliness rather than posing a question to/about the husband.

Porter.translator_strategy: Porter prioritizes a smoothly rhyming, metrically regular English lyric of plaintive loneliness over precise semantic and rhetorical fidelity to the original's pivot word and accusatory rhetorical question.

bipartite.note: The translation keeps the same two-part logic: lines 1-3 render the physical/emotional experience of sighing alone through the night till dawn, and lines 4-5 pivot to the rhetorical question addressed to the man, asking if he can realize how tedious it is. The inferential-sensory movement from lived sensation to accusatory question is maintained, though the reproachful edge is softened into a more neutral 'Can you realize'.

kakekotoba_handling.note: McCauley renders 夜 only as the literal temporal 'night' ('the long watch of the night'), losing the secondary sense of 夜 as one's life/lot/marriage condition; the pun collapses to a single literal reading.

kigo_handling.note: Consistent with the source analysis, no seasonal marker exists in the original and none is introduced in translation; 'night' and 'day' remain purely diurnal/temporal, not seasonal, images.

entries.content_summary: Sighing all alone — renders 嘆きつつ (sighing/grieving)

What a tedious thing it is — renders 久しきものとかは知る (how long/tedious a thing, do you know?)

line_mapping.structural_note: The translation follows the five-ku structure closely with a near one-to-one line-to-ku correspondence, expanding slightly into a rhetorical question form across the final two lines but preserving the overall bipartite division exactly.

McCauley.translator_strategy: McCauley aims for clear, literal, line-by-line fidelity to the surface narrative and rhetorical question of the poem, sacrificing the kakekotoba's double meaning for straightforward clarity.
